cells.tense: Endings are moving through you by consent, and nothing is being torn out.
cells.act: let an exchange flow both ways
cells.ask: Give a finished thing a real goodbye — a thank-you, a returned key, a last honest word. Then take back what you're owed, today.
cells.core:
Things are closing around you, and you're letting them close. Not because you're stoic about loss, but because you can feel when something has said what it came to say, and you'd rather see it off than keep it breathing on a machine. That's why what's arriving has somewhere to land — you keep clearing space without making a scene of the clearing. The leaving and the coming in are the same motion.

The part worth your attention now is the trade. When something ends, something also comes back to you: an hour, a room, an honest answer you'd stopped expecting. Say that out loud once this week. Hand back whatever you're holding that isn't yours, and take what is. The next thing at the door needs the room, and it needs you to be the one who calls the balance fair.
cells.sheetLine: You can end a thing and still take back what it owed you.
cells.verb: ending what is finished so the new can arrive
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside comes in

cells.tense: You will cut this loose before it has had a chance to be itself.
cells.act: feel it alongside them and keep your own side
cells.ask: When the urge to call something over arrives, sit with whoever else is in it before you decide. Feel what they carry. Then choose.
cells.core:
There's a way of moving on that is really just leaving early. You can feel the pull to close a role, a plan, the shape of a relationship, and the closing wears the face of freedom. It isn't. It's what staying long enough to be changed would cost, paid up in advance so you don't have to find out.

Stay in contact a bit past when the impulse speaks. When you want to call it finished, sit with the person or the situation first — let what they're carrying reach you, and keep your side while it does. You can feel someone without becoming them. And then, if it's still finished, close it. You'll be ending something real instead of something feared, and that's the whole difference. Only you can tell which one you're holding.
cells.sheetLine: Not every ending is freedom. Some are just leaving early.
cells.verb: ending what is finished so the new can arrive

cells.tense: A finished thing still has your weight on it, and you are leaning there.
cells.ask: Take a step away from something that's over — a call, a box, a road you keep retaking — ahead of feeling ready. Today, not later.
cells.core:
You've been keeping faith with something past its life. The faithfulness is real; it's aimed at the wrong thing. What's over doesn't need a guard, and leaning on its door spends the room the new thing would use. Stepping away isn't the same as saying it mattered less.

The way forward opens from motion first and feeling later. Go where something in you is already leaning, even a little, and trust the rest to show up once you've gone. Put energy you actually have into the direction you'd pick if the choice were free today. Direction doesn't arrive as certainty; it arrives as motion you can keep. Small and today beats whole and someday.
cells.sheetLine: Leaning on a finished door isn't loyalty. It's just still waiting.

cells.tense: Something is already ending in you, and it goes unnamed.
cells.act: give the mess a shape it can be carried in
cells.ask: Set down on one page what is actually leaving your life right now — plainly, nothing rearranged. That page is the container.
cells.core:
Something in you is rearranging, and it has been arriving as tiredness, or a busy stretch, or nothing in particular. You've been carrying the change around without knowing you were. Nothing's being hidden on purpose — the thing simply hasn't been put into a shape, so it moves through the days unnamed and spends you sideways.

Give it a container small enough to lift. One page, one list, one line — whatever is actually ending, set down flatly, with nothing tidied up. You don't have to act on any of it. The point is to move the thing out from under the description you've been using for it, so you're holding it rather than it holding the day. You'll know it's worked when the mess has an edge, and the edge is one you drew.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying a change that hasn't been written down yet.
cells.verb: ending what is finished so the new can arrive
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside comes in
